clue.text: Light-heavyweight, perhaps, from

parts.note: a boxer in the light-heavyweight class is literally light yet heavy, a slight fellow who is also large; 'from' points to the book's author, the answer at 28 across, whose number the print has lost

explanation.walkthrough: This is the title of Thomas Berger's 1964 novel of the Old West, the solution at 28 across; the cross-reference number after 'from' is missing in the printed clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Berger's novel takes its title from the nickname of its tiny narrator, a phrase that also suits a boxer weighing light-heavy.

clue.text: Redgauntlet

parts.note: the title of Walter Scott's 1824 novel, standing for the young hero it follows, Darsie, who turns out to be a Redgauntlet himself

explanation.walkthrough: Darsie Latimer is the hero of Scott's novel; he discovers he is really of the Redgauntlet family, so the novel's title names him.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's hero Darsie goes by this surname before learning his true Redgauntlet birth.

clue.text: Round song for goblin

definitions.meaning: to sing in a round, passing the tune from voice to voice, is an old verb sense
an ugly creature of Scandinavian folklore living under bridges or in caves

explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an old verb for singing a catch in parts and the name of a Norse folklore monster.

clue.text: Paying attention in Albee play

definitions.meaning: heeding what is said, present participle
Edward Albee's 1976 radio play of that title

explanation.surface: Someone attentive at an Edward Albee drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Heeding a speaker is what the word means, and Albee wrote a short play bearing it as its title.

clue.text: Titled privateer?

parts.note: 'titled' points to the written abbreviation for a baronet, a hereditary title; the privateer is the Welsh pirate Roberts, known as Black ___

explanation.surface: A pirate given a knighthood or peerage.
explanation.walkthrough: The written abbreviation after a baronet's name, the holder of a minor hereditary title, is also the nickname of the pirate John Roberts, called Black ___.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation follows a baronet's name, and it was the sobriquet of a notorious Caribbean pirate.

clue.text: Shakespearean setter from mugger's haunt

definitions.meaning: in Henry IV Part 1 Poins calls this thief 'our setter', the man who spots victims for a robbery
the hill in Kent where Falstaff and his gang rob travellers

explanation.surface: A crossword compiler hailing from a thieves' hideout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' looks like a crossword compiler; it is Elizabethan slang for a robbers' scout. Gad's Hill near Rochester was notorious for highwaymen, and Dickens later lived there.
explanation.definitionFit: The character in Henry IV who sets up the robbery shares his name with the Kentish hill where it happens.

clue.text: Tess's was not much of a guardian

definitions.text: Tess's was not much of a guardian

parts.words: Tess's was not much of a guardian
parts.note: Tess of the d'Urbervilles marries Clare, who abandons her; a protective spirit is called a guardian one of these

explanation.surface: A young woman's protector failed her badly.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hardy's novel Tess's husband is Angel Clare, who deserts her on their wedding night; the clue plays on the phrase guardian angel.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's Clare bears this forename, and a guardian spirit watching over someone is called one.

clue.text: Protector of play by WS (1602)?

definitions.meaning: Oliver held the title Lord Protector of England
The True Chronicle History of Thomas Lord ___ was published in 1602 as by 'W.S.', inviting attribution to Shakespeare

explanation.surface: A guardian figure from a drama of 1602 by Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1602 play about Henry VIII's minister Thomas was printed with the initials W.S., and is part of the Shakespeare apocrypha; Oliver of the same surname was Lord Protector.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver of that surname ruled as Lord Protector, and Henry VIII's minister Thomas is the subject of the 1602 play.

clue.text: Syphon out sleepy god

indicators.note: 'out' says the letters of the word Syphon are put out of their order

explanation.surface: Drain a siphon until the drowsy deity appears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' turns the letters of SYPHON into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth he is the god of sleep, twin of Thanatos, death.

clue.text: Clad, like Prufrock, or Tressell's benefactor

definitions.text: Clad, like Prufrock, or Tressell's benefactor

parts.words: Clad, like Prufrock, or Tressell's benefactor
parts.note: Eliot's Prufrock will 'wear the bottoms of my trousers rolled'; Robert Tressell wrote The Ragged ___ Philanthropists, a philanthropist being a benefactor

explanation.surface: Dressed like Eliot's timid hero, or like a working-class novel's generous figures.
explanation.walkthrough: Both literary references point at legwear: Prufrock's rolled trouser bottoms, and the ragged painters of Tressell's novel about Edwardian Hastings.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means wearing breeches, as Prufrock does, and it is the middle word of Tressell's novel title.

clue.text: Russian writer shows ruler in bloody surroundings

indicators.note: 'in' places the ruler within the bloody surroundings

parts.note: bloody means gory, here forming the outside
K is the abbreviation for king, as in chess

explanation.surface: A Russian author depicts a monarch amid scenes of carnage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts K, a king, inside GORY.
explanation.definitionFit: Maxim, author of The Lower Depths and Mother, took this pen name, which means 'bitter' in Russian.

clue.text: Red-bearded bagpiper who went the old Kent road

definitions.text: Red-bearded bagpiper who went the old Kent road

parts.words: Red-bearded bagpiper who went the old Kent road
parts.note: Chaucer's pilgrim with a red beard plays the bagpipes as the company ride out of Southwark towards Canterbury

explanation.surface: A ginger-bearded piper walking the old road through Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: In the General Prologue of The Canterbury Tales this pilgrim has a red beard and 'a baggepipe wel koude he blowe'; the pilgrims took the old road from London into Kent, recalling the Old Kent Road in south London.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaucer's rowdy pilgrim, who tells a bawdy tale, is this grain-grinding tradesman.

clue.text: Greek playwright in Bible book?

definitions.meaning: a poet of Athenian New Comedy, rival of Menander
Paul's short letter to a Colossian master about his slave Onesimus

explanation.surface: A Greek dramatist inside a volume of scripture.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to the New Comedy dramatist and to the recipient of Paul's shortest epistle.

clue.text: Win back Giono novel?

definitions.meaning: Jean Giono's 1930 novel of a Provençal village restored to life, translated as Harvest

explanation.surface: Recovering a book by Jean Giono.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means recover what was lost, and Giono used the identical French word as his novel's title.

clue.text: Kipling's superior

parts.note: Kipling's soldier-narrator tells the water-carrier 'You're a better man than I am'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Superior' looks like a boss or officer; Kipling's poem ends with the speaker admitting the regimental water-bearer is the better man.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indian water-carrier of the poem is the one the soldier calls a better man than himself.

clue.text: Dickens's Flemish nurse?

parts.note: a character in Dickens shares the name of the Flemish-speaking region of Belgium, so the question mark casts her as Flemish

explanation.surface: A nanny from Belgium in a Dickens novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The region of Belgium where Flemish is spoken gives its name to a Dickens figure, so the question mark marks the playful 'Flemish'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Flemish-speaking north of Belgium is this region, which also serves as a surname in Dickens.

clue.text: Indefinite postponement threatened by Corvus corax

definitions.meaning: 'not ever again', putting something off for good
Corvus corax is the common raven, whose one word in Poe's poem is this refrain

explanation.surface: A raven menacingly announces that something is off forever.
explanation.walkthrough: Corvus corax is the Latin name of the raven; in Poe's The Raven the bird answers every question with the same ominous word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means never again, and is the refrain croaked by Poe's raven.

clue.text: Go admire sort of symbol

indicators.note: 'sort of' tells us to sort the letters of Go admire into another order

explanation.surface: Encouragement to admire a particular kind of sign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges GOADMIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A written character standing for an idea, as in Chinese script, is this kind of sign.

clue.text: J. T. Edson's sort of eager end

definitions.note: a possessive standing for a title by the Western writer

indicators.note: 'sort of' tells us to sort the letters of eager end into another order

explanation.surface: The keen finale typical of a writer of Westerns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges EAGEREND. J. T. Edson was a prolific British author of Western paperbacks, one of which bears this title.
explanation.definitionFit: A turncoat or outlaw figure of the Western genre gives Edson's book its title.

clue.text: Writer from French roots

definitions.meaning: Jean, the seventeenth-century French tragedian of Phèdre
the French word for root, plural in the clue but singular in the word itself

explanation.surface: An author of French origin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from French roots' suggests a writer's ancestry; it is the French word for 'root'.
explanation.definitionFit: The French tragedian's surname is the ordinary French noun meaning root.

clue.text: "Endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been and are being -d" (Darwin)

definitions.text: "Endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been and are being -d" (Darwin)

parts.words: "Endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been and are being -d" (Darwin)
parts.note: the closing words of On the Origin of Species, with the final verb left to fill in

explanation.surface: A quotation from Darwin with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The last sentence of On the Origin of Species ends 'endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved'; the '-d' asks for the verb without its ending.
explanation.definitionFit: Darwin's word for species developing over generations is the verb meaning develop gradually.

clue.text: Where seducers lurk, Vita Sackville-West seems to warn

definitions.text: Where seducers lurk, Vita Sackville-West seems to warn

parts.words: Where seducers lurk, Vita Sackville-West seems to warn
parts.note: Vita Sackville-West's 1924 novella is titled Seducers in ___, as if warning of a place

explanation.surface: A novelist cautions against a place full of tempters.
explanation.walkthrough: The novella's title, Seducers in Ecuador, reads like a warning about a South American country, though the book barely concerns it.
explanation.definitionFit: The South American republic named in the title of Sackville-West's novella is where the seducers are placed.

clue.text: Pedlar's offering must be a biography, according to E. C. Bentley's dictum

definitions.meaning: a cheap pamphlet of ballads or tales sold by itinerant chapmen

definitions.text: a biography, according to E. C. Bentley's dictum
definitions.meaning: Bentley's clerihew says 'Biography is about chaps', so a biography is a volume about fellows

explanation.surface: A travelling seller's wares must be a life story, says a famous rhyme.
explanation.walkthrough: E. C. Bentley's clerihew runs 'Geography is about maps, But Biography is about chaps'; chaps are men, and a book about them gives the second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Chapmen, door-to-door pedlars, sold small printed pamphlets of this name; Bentley's rhyme makes it a book about men.

clue.text: We hear Wodehouse butler in the wood

indicators.note: 'We hear' signals the word is judged by how it sounds when spoken

parts.note: the butler at Blandings Castle in P. G. Wodehouse's stories is Sebastian Beach

explanation.surface: Listening out for a Wodehouse butler among the trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'We hear' turns BEACH, the Blandings butler, into a tree with the same sound.
explanation.definitionFit: The smooth grey-barked tree gives a pale hardwood used for furniture.

clue.text: It may be a feeling of guilt, they say

definitions.text: It may be a feeling of guilt, they say

parts.words: It may be a feeling of guilt, they say
parts.note: guilt and gilt sound alike, so a 'feeling of guilt' is something with a gilded feel, a gold-coloured decorative alloy

explanation.surface: Remorse, people tell us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a feeling of guilt' looks like remorse; spoken, guilt sounds like gilt, and this gilded bronze has the look and feel of gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Gilded bronze or brass used to decorate clocks and furniture has a gold surface, the gilt of the pun.

clue.text: Nothing above standard in prison camp

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'above' places the first piece on top of the second

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O
a standard is a banner or flag

explanation.surface: Nothing rises higher than the flag over a detention camp.
explanation.definitionFit: German camps for captured officers in the Second World War were known by this short term.

clue.text: Wyndham Lewis recorded those of God

definitions.text: Wyndham Lewis recorded those of God

parts.words: Wyndham Lewis recorded those of God
parts.note: Wyndham Lewis's 1930 satirical novel is The ___ of God

explanation.surface: A modernist painter-writer documented God's own creatures.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewis's satire The Apes of God mocks the Bloomsbury set as imitators of real artists.
explanation.definitionFit: Primates such as gorillas are these, and Lewis used the word for the dilettante imitators in his satire.

clue.text: Their wings made this for MacKinlay Kantor

definitions.text: Their wings made this for MacKinlay Kantor

parts.words: Their wings made this for MacKinlay Kantor
parts.note: Kantor's 1938 book is The ___ of Their Wings

explanation.surface: Birds' wings sounding out for an American novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: MacKinlay Kantor, author of Andersonville, wrote The Noise of Their Wings, about passenger pigeons; the printed clue lacks its letter count.
explanation.definitionFit: Flapping wings make a sound, the word that completes Kantor's title.

clue.text: Folk in the red provided inhabitants again

indicators.note: 'in' says the folk are placed inside the red

parts.note: taken as written, the colour red
folk means people

explanation.surface: Communist folk resettled an emptied land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the red' supplies the colour as written; a communist is also a red, which colours the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To fill an area again with residents after it was emptied is to restock it with population.

clue.text: Nowhere was his work much appreciated

definitions.text: Nowhere was his work much appreciated

parts.words: Nowhere was his work much appreciated
parts.note: read as 'his book Nowhere was much admired', not as a complaint that he was neglected everywhere

explanation.surface: A writer whose work found favour nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nowhere' looks like a lament for an ignored writer; it is the title of this American novelist's 1985 book.
explanation.definitionFit: The American novelist who wrote Little Big Man also published a novel called Nowhere.
